chunks.title: Welcome to Replit Learn
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
Replit Learn
Build with confidence.
A practical learning path from a blank idea to a production-ready application.
Learn how Replit projects fit together, how the Workspace supports your work, and how to build, publish, and share an app.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
An app is a tool or service that helps someone get something done. It can help a person organise work, make a decision, create something, or help a business serve its customers.
Explain what an app does in plain language
Name the core parts that make an app work
Describe how those parts work together
In Replit, you can begin with a plain-language description of the service you want to provide. Agent can help turn that idea into a working project, and you can inspect the screens, code, data, and published result in one place.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: An app helps someone do something
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Apps exist to provide a useful service. A calendar app helps people plan time. A shop helps people find and buy something. A project tool helps a team organise work. Some apps are for one person, while others help a business serve many people. What matters is that the app has a purpose and helps someone make progress.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: Most apps use a few core parts
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You do not need to know how to build every part yet. For now, it helps to know what each part is responsible for.
Frontend and UI: the screens, buttons, forms, and messages that people see and use.
Backend and logic: the behind-the-scenes work, including rules, decisions, and actions.
Data: the information an app remembers, such as accounts, projects, messages, settings, or orders.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: Some apps need more pieces
chunks.text:
App Foundations
As an app becomes more useful, it may also need file storage for images or documents, sign-in for personal accounts, payments, or connections to other services. These are useful additions, not requirements for every first version.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: The parts work together
chunks.text:
App Foundations
When someone takes an action, the frontend collects it and shows the result. The backend performs the work that should happen behind the scenes. Data helps the app remember what happened. The diagram below shows that simple path.

chunks.title: What Is an App?
chunks.heading: You can start small
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You do not need to understand every part before you begin. Start with one useful idea, build a small version, and add the pieces your app needs as you learn. The next chapters introduce each building block one at a time.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
An app begins as instructions written in code. A project keeps those instructions in files, so the different parts of an app can stay organised and work together.
Explain the relationship between code, files, and a project
Recognise why an app uses more than one file
Describe how a framework helps organise an app
A Replit project gives you one place to see the files behind an app, run it, and preview the result. As you explore a project, notice that the file tree is an organised map of the work—not a list you need to understand all at once.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: Code is a set of instructions
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Code tells an app what to show, what to do when someone takes an action, and how to work with information. You do not need to read or write every line to understand the basic idea: code is the written set of instructions behind an app.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: A project keeps the work together
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A project is the home for an app and the work that supports it. It holds the code, files, settings, and other resources needed to build, run, and improve that app. Keeping related work together makes a project easier to understand and change over time.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: Files organise work by responsibility
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Most apps use many files because one large file becomes difficult to follow. Files can be organised around a screen, a reusable part of the interface, backend logic, a connection to data, or a setting. The exact structure differs between projects, but the purpose is always the same: give each piece of work a clear home.
A UI component file might describe a button, form, or screen.
A backend file might handle a request or apply a business rule.
A data file might describe how the app reads or saves information.
A configuration file might tell the project how to run or publish.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: Frameworks provide a shared structure
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A framework is a set of helpful conventions and tools for building an app. It gives a project a predictable way to organise screens, routes, shared components, and other common needs. This means builders do not have to invent the structure from scratch every time.

chunks.title: Projects, Code & Files
chunks.heading: You only need the map for now
chunks.text:
App Foundations
At this stage, you do not need to memorise a project’s files. It is enough to recognise that an app is organised work: instructions live in files, files live in a project, and the project brings the pieces together into something people can use. Later, you will explore how AI agents can work with this same project structure.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The frontend is the part of an app that people see and use. It turns an app’s purpose into screens, controls, information, and feedback that help someone get something done.
Explain what the frontend and UI are
Recognise the roles of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
Identify the key states a helpful interface should show
Use Replit Design to explore a screen before you commit to code. You can ask Agent to create a first version, compare variations, and refine the experience. Then use Preview to try the task as a builder would, including loading, empty, and error states.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: The frontend is the part people use
chunks.text:
App Foundations
When someone opens an app, reads a message, fills in a form, or taps a button, they are using the frontend. The frontend gives people a way to take action and see the result. It is the part of the app that makes the service feel clear and usable.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: The UI guides someone through a task
chunks.text:
App Foundations
UI means user interface. It includes the screens, buttons, forms, labels, menus, and messages that appear in an app. A good UI makes the next step easy to find. It explains what someone can do, what is happening now, and what happened after they acted.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Frontend code has a few familiar jobs
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You do not need to write this code yet. It is enough to know the role each part usually plays.
HTML gives a screen its structure, such as headings, text, forms, and buttons.
CSS controls how the screen looks, including layout, spacing, colours, and typography.
JavaScript makes the screen respond to actions, such as opening a menu, checking a form, or showing new information.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Helpful interfaces show their state
chunks.text:
App Foundations
An app changes as someone uses it. It may have no information yet, be waiting for something to load, show a result, confirm success, or explain a problem. Showing those states helps people understand the app instead of leaving them to guess.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Feedback is part of the experience
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Feedback is not decoration. A loading message tells someone the app is working. A confirmation tells them their action succeeded. A clear error message helps them recover. Small signals like these make an app feel calm, trustworthy, and easier to use.

chunks.title: Frontend & UI
chunks.heading: Start with one clear task
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You do not need a perfect interface before you begin. Pick one action the app should help someone complete, make that action easy to find, and show a useful result. You can improve the details as you learn from real use.

chunks.title: Backend & Logic
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The backend handles work that should not happen only in the browser, including rules, workflows, and communication with data or outside services.
When you ask Agent to add a feature in Replit, it can work across the interface and server code together. Review the changes as one workflow rather than treating the frontend and backend as unrelated projects.

chunks.title: Backend & Logic
chunks.heading: Put decisions in the right place
chunks.text:
App Foundations
The backend checks what is allowed, decides what happens next, and protects work that should not be controlled by the interface alone. This can include processing a payment, deciding who can edit a project, or sending an email.

chunks.title: Backend & Logic
chunks.heading: APIs are contracts
chunks.text:
App Foundations
An API is a structured agreement for exchanging information. Your frontend asks for something in a predictable way; the backend returns a predictable response. Clear contracts make a system easier to change and debug.

chunks.title: Backend & Logic
chunks.heading: Build one workflow at a time
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Start with a single request from beginning to end. Once it works, you can add validation, errors, permissions, and more complex behavior without losing the thread.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Databases help apps remember structured information that needs to be searched, updated, and connected to other records.
Replit Database gives you a place to add persistent records as an idea becomes a useful product. Agent can help you sketch the model, but you should still decide what the app needs to remember.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: Model what matters
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Begin by naming the things your app needs to remember: people, projects, messages, orders, or preferences. Then identify how those records relate. This is a product decision before it becomes a technical one.

chunks.title: Databases
chunks.heading: Use a database for records
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Databases are for information you need to search, filter, update, and connect. A project table, for example, can link a project to its creator and its tasks.

chunks.title: File Storage
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
File storage gives an app a durable home for images, documents, audio, video, and other larger files that do not fit naturally into a database record.
Use Replit Object Storage when your project needs to keep files such as images or documents. Pair it with Replit Database to store the references and metadata that make those files useful in your app.

chunks.title: File Storage
chunks.heading: Files are different from records
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A profile picture, invoice, or uploaded video is useful information, but it is not the same as a name, date, or status. Files can be large, varied, and expensive to move, so apps store them differently from structured records.

chunks.title: File Storage
chunks.heading: Connect files to your data
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A database record can keep a reference to a file in storage. That lets the app answer useful questions: who uploaded it, which project it belongs to, whether it is public, and when it should appear.

chunks.title: File Storage
chunks.heading: Decide what people can access
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Before adding uploads, decide who can add, view, replace, or remove a file. This keeps storage aligned with the identity and permissions model of your app.

chunks.title: Users & Access
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Identity lets an app know who someone is. Authentication verifies that identity, while permissions decide what that person can see or do.
Replit can help you add an authentication flow as part of a project. Later, in Secure and Monitor, you will learn how to protect secrets and review permissions more deeply.

chunks.title: Users & Access
chunks.heading: Identity creates ownership
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Accounts let people return to saved work, collaborate, and trust that their information belongs to them. Even a simple app often needs a clear answer to: who is this person?

chunks.title: Users & Access
chunks.heading: Authentication and authorization differ
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Authentication answers “are you who you say you are?” Authorization answers “are you allowed to do this?” Keeping those questions separate makes it easier to reason about access.

chunks.title: Users & Access
chunks.heading: Start with the smallest useful role model
chunks.text:
App Foundations
A product may only need an owner and a collaborator at first. Add more roles only when they represent a real difference in responsibility or access.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Integrations let an app use capabilities such as payments, email, maps, analytics, and AI without rebuilding those systems from scratch.
In Replit, Agent can help connect an external service to your project, but you still decide the product flow: when the connection is needed, what data moves, and what the app should do if it fails.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Extend the core experience
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Choose integrations that directly support the job your app helps someone do. A calendar connection may be essential to a scheduling product, while payments may be unnecessary until someone is ready to buy.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Plan for the outside world
chunks.text:
App Foundations
External services can be slow, unavailable, or return unexpected results. A resilient app explains what happened, keeps important work recoverable, and does not assume every request will succeed.

chunks.title: Integrations
chunks.heading: Keep boundaries clear
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Use the backend to manage credentials and communicate with sensitive services. This helps you protect secrets and gives your product one dependable place to handle errors.

chunks.title: App Architecture
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
App Foundations
App architecture is the way the interface, logic, data, identity, and integrations work together to deliver a reliable experience.
Replit keeps your project, preview, code, services, and publishing workflow close together. That makes it easier to trace one journey and decide where a new capability belongs before you ask Agent to build it.

chunks.title: App Architecture
chunks.heading: Trace a single journey
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Pick one meaningful action, such as creating a project or sending a message. Follow it from the screen, through the backend, into data or services, and back to the person. This reveals how your app is actually organized.

chunks.title: App Architecture
chunks.heading: Make the boundaries visible
chunks.text:
App Foundations
Clear boundaries help you change an app safely. Keep interface concerns, business rules, data access, and external connections understandable rather than hiding everything in one place.

chunks.title: App Architecture
chunks.heading: Grow through iteration
chunks.text:
App Foundations
You do not need a perfect architecture before you begin. Build a simple, complete workflow, learn from real use, then improve the pieces that need to carry more responsibility.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
AI is a broad term for systems that perform tasks associated with perception, language, prediction, or decision-making. In this course, you will focus on AI that works with language and helps people create, analyze, and act.
Use Agent in Replit as a practical example: you describe an outcome in language, then collaborate with an AI system that can explore and change a project.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: What it is
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
AI is a broad term for systems that perform tasks associated with perception, language, prediction, or decision-making. In this course, you will focus on AI that works with language and helps people create, analyze, and act.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: Why it matters
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
Understanding what AI can and cannot help with is the practical reason to learn this. It helps you design AI features with intent instead of treating a model like magic. The aim is a useful, bounded experience that people can understand and trust. The point is not to memorise a term. It is to recognise when this idea can make a task clearer, safer, or more useful for the person doing the work.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: What it is for
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
Use What Is AI? to make one part of a workflow more intentional. Begin with a real need, state what a helpful result looks like, and keep the first version small enough to inspect. A focused first attempt gives you something concrete to improve instead of a vague feeling that the work should be “more advanced.”

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: Where it fits
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
In a real product, an AI model sits behind a clear interface and a thoughtful workflow. People provide information, the model helps with a defined task, and your app makes the result easy to review or use.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: In practice
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
AI is useful when the task has patterns to recognise, language to work with, or options to explore. It is less useful when a decision needs a guaranteed factual answer without any way to check it. Treat it as a capable collaborator: give it a bounded job, inspect the result, and decide what happens next.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: What to notice
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
Pay attention to the hand-off between a person and the system. What do they provide? What does the app or agent do next? What feedback tells them that the result is ready, incomplete, or needs a different approach? Those moments are where a concept becomes a usable experience.

chunks.title: What Is AI?
chunks.heading: Give it a try
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
Choose one work task you know well—summarising feedback, drafting a reply, or sorting requests. Describe the input, the helpful output, and one example that would show the result is not good enough yet.

chunks.title: Models & LLMs
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
A model is a trained system that turns inputs into outputs. A large language model, or LLM, is trained to understand and generate language, which makes it useful for conversation, writing, analysis, and code.
When you choose an AI capability for a Replit project, the model is the engine behind the experience. Choose based on the task, quality, speed, and cost.

chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
AI Foundations
AI systems respond to the information you give them. Inputs can include text, images, files, or structured data; outputs can be language, classifications, code, or a suggested next action.
In a Replit app, define the input a person provides and the output they need. Clear boundaries make an AI feature easier to test and improve.

chunks.text:

Ask Agent to help draft a prompt, then test it against real examples in your Replit project. Treat the prompt as product behavior you can refine.
